A 61-year-old gas station employee first noted tingling in the lat-
eral aspects of his thighs. Nine days later, he woke up with mus-
cle stiffness and painful spasms of both legs. The stiffness and
spasms worsened and soon he was unable to walk. Three days
later, he was admitted for evaluation. His past medical history was
unremarkable. There were no symptoms suggestive of infection
prior to the illness. Vital signs were normal, except for mild ele-
vation of body temperature to 37.8° C. He was conscious and an
examination of cranial nerve function revealed no abnormalities.
He complained of diplopia, but no limitation of extraocular move-
ment was noted. The muscles of the lower trunk and lower limbs
exhibited marked and “board-like” rigidity with the hip and knee
joints fixed in partial flexion, and the ankle joints in pronounced
plantar flexion. Paroxysmal, painful spasms of the lower trunk
and lower limbs were easily induced by noise or touch. No tris-
mus or fasciculations were observed. The effect of sleep on rigid-
ity was uncertain. Deep tendon reflexes in the lower limbs were
unremarkable. Upper limbs showed normal muscle tone and re-
flexes. No pathological reflexes, sensory deficits or incoordina-
tion were noted. Laboratory examination revealed mild leukocy-
tosis and elevated creatine kinase (CK) (976 IU/l), but normal
serum C-reactive protein. No evidence of diabetes mellitus was
found. Cerebrospinal fluid examination revealed a mild leukocy-
tosis of 41/ml
3 (lymphocyte/neutrophil = 40/1). IgG index was
normal. Anti-65-kDa GAD antibody in the serum was mildly ele-
vated, to 22 U/ml (normal ≤ 15 U/ml; ELISA; Biomate). Anti-
HTLV-I antibody was negative. Needle electromyography (EMG)
on the second hospital day showed normal spontaneous motor unit
potentials, except in the left gastrocnemius muscle where high
amplitude potentials were recorded. Surface EMG of the lower
limbs revealed continuous muscle discharges, which were super-
imposed with paroxysmal and synchronous discharges of antago-
nistic muscles. Intravenous diazepam led to a complete but tran-
sient remission of the symptoms. The characteristics of stiffness
and spasms, the elevated anti-GAD antibody, the EMG findings,
and the effectiveness of diazepam pointed to a diagnosis of SMS.
The stiffness and spasms continued to worsen during the first hos-
pital week. The CK and myoglobin levels in the serum were ele-
vated to 7989 IU/l and above 500 ng/ml, respectively. Secondary
renal failure, marked fluctuations of blood pressure and heart rate,
and respiratory failure ensued. Intensive therapy, with hemodialy-
sis and plasmapheresis, relieved the renal and respiratory failure,
and the CK levels in the serum were normalized. The patient be-
came alert and vital signs stabilized. In the following 2 weeks, the
stiffness and spasms subsided, but moderate atrophy and flaccid-
ity of the lower truncal and gluteal muscles as well as those of
lower limbs, particularly in their proximal portions, became ap-
parent. The upper limbs remained intact and no sensory distur-
bance was noted. The subsequent clinical course was complicated

by pneumonia and pseudomembranous enterocolitis. Although the
patient had been recovering from these complications, he died of
unexpected, sudden respiratory arrest 5 weeks after the onset of
the symptoms. An autopsy was performed 4.7 h post mortem.
Histological and immunohistochemical studies
All tissues removed at autopsy were fixed in 10% buffered forma-
lin and processed for paraffin sectioning and staining with hema-
toxylin and eosin (H&E), Bodian silver, Klüver-Barrera (KB) and
Holzer. Using the avidin-biotin peroxidase complex method, rep-
resentative sections were immunostained using antisera directed
against glial fibrillary acid protein (GFAP; Dako, Carpinteria,
Calif.; diluted 1:400), GABA (Sigma, St. Louis, Mo., 1:2000) and
GAD (Chemicon, Temecula, Calif., 1:2000). Four subjects (aver-
age 69 years: range 59–73 years, postmortem examination per-
formed after an average delay of 3.8 h) without spinal involvement
served as controls.
Quantitative analyses
Specimens for quantitative analyses were taken from the cervical
(C7), thoracic (T11) and lumbar (L3 and L5) spinal cord seg-
ments. Seven serial 10- mm-thick sections from the rostral end of
each segment were obtained. The first, fourth and seventh step-
sections were subjected to KB staining. In these sections, the ven-
tral horn of the spinal cord, which is defined as the gray matter
anterior to the horizontal line running through the ventral tip of
posterior funiculi, was targeted for evaluation (Fig. 1). Multiple
photomicrographs covering the entire ventral horn of the spinal
cord were taken and the photoimages were input through the film
scanner (Quickscan 35, Minolta, Tokyo, Japan) into the micro-
computer (Macintosh; PowerBook 540c) and analyzed using a
software system (MacScope, Mitani, Fukui, Japan). The analysis
was limited to neurons with conspicuous nucleoli and Nissl’s
substance. The area of the ventral horn of the spinal cord was
measured, the number of neurons was counted and the density of
neurons was calculated. The somal area of neurons was measured
by tracing the soma manually. Neuronal processes were traced to
the point where the Nissl’s substance was recognized. In each
case, the photoimages of GAD-like immunoreactive granules in
ten randomized, high-power fields of the ventral horn of the
spinal cord were digitized as binary images, and the fractional
area density of immunoreactive granules was obtained. The den-
sity of Purkinje cells was calculated as the number of cells per
unit length of Purkinje cell layer (no./mm). The measurement of
Purkinje cells was performed in 10- mm-thick horizontal sections
of the dorsal cerebellar hemisphere at the level of the dentate nu-
cleus, and low-power microscopic fields, 20 in the SMS patient
and 5 each in the control subjects (totaling 20) were randomly se-
lected.

Pathological study

mild, restricted pneumonia, a small gastric ulcer and mem-
branous coagula with an inflammatory cell infiltration in
the hyperemic colonic mucosa. The pancreas, including

the islets of Langerhans, was unremarkable. No evidence
of malignancy was noted. The muscles of the trunk and
lower limbs exhibited moderate diffuse atrophy. The brain
weighed 1480 g and showed mild ventricular dilatation.
The spinal cord was unremarkable. Microscopic examina-
tion revealed moderate fibrillary gliosis in the cerebral
periventricular white matter and periaqueductal region. The
oculomotor and trochlear nuclei and the substantia nigra
exhibited no apparent neuronal loss. The dorsal efferent
nucleus of vagus showed mild gliosis. The spinal cord
was histologically evaluated in the lower cervical (C6–8),
thoracic (T1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11), lumbar (L1–5) and sacral
(S1–4) segments. In the intermediate zone and the medial
part of ventral horn in all segments studied, the number of
neurons markedly decreased and the neuropil was rarefied
compared with the controls (Fig. 2a, b). Some of the large
motor neurons in the lumbar segments showed central
chromatolytic changes (Fig. 2d) and vacuolation. The in-
termediate lateral nucleus and Clarke’s column were unre-
markable. The corticospinal tract appeared normal bilater-
ally. On Holzer’s staining and GFAP immunostaining,
marked fibrillary gliosis was observed around the central
canal through all segments (Fig. 2e). Gliosis was also ob-
served in the ventral half of the posterior funiculi, pre-
dominantly in the lumbar segments, and in the ventral
horns (Fig. 2e). Parenchymal and leptomeningeal perivas-
cular lymphocyte cuffing (PVLC) was observed in the
brain stem and spinal cord, but was only focal and mild
(Fig. 2c). GAD-like immunoreactivity was recognized as
punctate granules mainly in the neuropil as well as around
the soma of large motor neurons (Fig. 3). The pattern of
immunostaining appeared not to be different from that of
controls. Moderate neurogenic atrophy was noted in the
intercostal and quadriceps femoris muscles. Multiple soli-
tary or small-grouped small angulated fibers and a few
targetoid or hypertrophic fibers were observed (Fig. 2f).
No PVLC was noted in the muscles. The peripheral nerves
were not available for pathological evaluations.
Quantitative analyses
For a precise size-distribution study, we chose the somal
area to represent neuronal cell size. However, since pre-
vious studies in the literature have used a somal diame-
ter for this purpose, we first evaluated the correlation
between the somal diameter and somal area. In the con-
trols, a statistically significant regression coefficient ( P
< 0.0001) was obtained between the somal diameter and
the somal area in the neurons in the ventral horn of the
spinal cord in all four segments studied (C7, T11, L3,
L5) (Fig. 4). We then compared the neuronal density of
neurons in the ventral horn, in the SMS patient and in
controls (Table 1). The density of neurons with a somal

loss in the basal ganglia has not been described in SMS pa-
tients, either with or without anti-GAD antibodies. Cere-
bellar ataxia or cerebellar degeneration is also extremely
rare in SMS [12]. Our SMS patient showed no pathological
abnormality in the basal ganglia and substantia nigra, and
had no significant reduction in the density of Purkinje cells.
Pancreatic beta cells are also known to contain GAD,
and are considered to be autoimmune targets in insulin-
dependent diabetes mellitus (IDDM). There are two iso-
forms of GAD, i.e., 65-kDa GAD and 67-kDa GAD. In
IDDM, anti-GAD antibodies are directed primarily against
the 65-kDa GAD isoforms [14, 16, 20, 40], which are
found in 75% of IDDM patients [16]. The 65-kDa GAD is
also the primary isoform associated with SMS [6]. How-
ever, only a small proportion of IDDM patients develops
SMS, despite IDDM being a common disease. Our SMS
patient did not have any evidence of IDDM. Recently, an-
tibodies other than against GAD have been demonstrated
in SMS patients with breast cancer [8, 11]. Evidence of
inflammation, including PVLC, in SMS has been consid-
ered to support an autoimmune basis for SMS [26, 28, 41].
However, there were cases with mild or no inflammatory
reactions [24, 39, 43]. Our SMS patient showed only mild
inflammatory changes, although the treatment may have
suppressed inflammation.
The acute clinical presentation, the symptomatic re-
sponse to plasmapheresis and the existence of elevated
titer of anti-GAD antibody in the serum in our SMS pa-
tient suggest a likely inflammatory or autoimmune basis
for the illness. On the other hand, the reduction in the den-
sity of smaller a -motor neurons and g-motor neurons, the
chromatolytic changes in the larger a -motor neurons, and
the preservation of spinal GAD-like immunoreactivity and
of non-spinal GAD-containing neurons are clearly sug-
gestive of the influence of some factors other than au-
toimmune mechanisms involving anti-GAD antibodies.
The occurrence of SMS without anti-GAD antibodies,
IDDM patients, positive for anti-GAD antibodies without
SMS, and some documented cases with mild or no in-
flammatory reactions also support this assumption. Thus,
more diverse pathomechanisms are probably associated
with the disease processes of SMS. Collection and analy-
ses of well-documented SMS cases are needed for the fur-
ther understanding of this rare neuromuscular disorder.
